raw_response.headline_result_summary: Using 2001 and 2011 Census of India data on N = 3,547 statutory cities and towns nested within 21 states, Subramanyam (2020) models 10-year percentage-point growth in household in-residence municipal tap-water coverage (mean +5.08 pp; positive growth in 68% of cities) across three multilevel governance dimensions, finding mixed institutional/fiscal results: (1) Headline local government capacity / statutory status finding: Higher local government administrative capacity (Municipal corporation status / Metropolitan city size) is favorably associated with household tap-water coverage expansion, whereas subordinate urban local government tiers lag significantly—Municipalities (-4.062***, SE = 1.254) and Town panchayats (-4.034***, SE = 1.540) recorded ~4.0 percentage points less coverage growth than Municipal corporations (Model 2), and Small cities (-5.122**, SE = 2.011) and Small towns (-5.432**, SE = 2.209) recorded ~5.1-5.4 percentage points less growth than Metropolitan cities (Model 1; Medium cities were null at -2.238, SE = 2.504); (2) Intergovernmental fiscal transfers: Per-capita water infrastructure grant aid under NURM/UIDSSMT is significantly negatively associated with household tap-water coverage growth (-0.034**, SE = 0.015 in both models; unfavorable to household coverage expansion, attributed to spending on bulk/technology upgrades rather than household connections); and (3) State-level fiscal decentralization: The state fiscal decentralization index (municipal own-source revenue share of state GDP) has a statistically null association with city water coverage growth (magnitude 2.011, SE = 3.949 in Model 1; 2.016, SE = 3.936 in Model 2). State NSDP per capita is positively associated with coverage growth (+0.001***, +1.0 pp per Rs. 1,000 per capita).
raw_response.specification_or_coding_pitfalls: 1. CRITICAL PDF MINUS-SIGN EXTRACTION ARTIFACT IN TABLE 4 (PDF p. 11): IWA Publishing's PDF font encoding drops minus signs ('-') in Table 4 (and substitutes '¼' for '=', ',' for '<', and '.' for '>' in Tables 1-4). Consequently, negative coefficients in Table 4 appear without minus signs in raw extracted text ('0.173***' for 2001 baseline coverage, '0.034**' for Intergovernmental aid, '5.122**' for Small city, '5.432**' for Small town, '4.062***' for Municipality, and '4.034***' for Town panchayat). Reading Table 4 without cross-checking Table 3 and the main-text prose (PDF pp. 8, 10-12) would catastrophically flip the sign of every statistically significant governance and policy coefficient—especially falsely coding NURM/UIDSSMT intergovernmental aid as positive (+0.034**) when the author explicitly reports it is significantly negative! 2. REFERENCE-CATEGORY SIGN INVERSION ON LOCAL CAPACITY: Table 4 sets the highest-capacity categories (Metropolitan city in Model 1; Municipal corporation in Model 2) as the omitted reference groups, so the lower-capacity dummy coefficients (Municipality -4.062***, Town panchayat -4.034***, Small city -5.122**, Small town -5.432**) carry negative raw signs even though higher local government administrative capacity is substantively favorable to household water access (equivalently, subordinate small-town ULB status is unfavorable/lagging). 3. MULTIPLE GOVERNANCE MECHANISMS WITH DIVERGENT DIRECTIONS: Depending on whether a synthesis extracts local municipal administrative capacity (favorable for higher capacity / unfavorable for lower-tier status), intergovernmental grant aid via NURM/UIDSSMT (unfavorable, -0.034**), or state fiscal decentralization (null, p >= 0.10), the direction differs sharply. 4. MINOR SAMPLE COUNT DISCREPANCY: Category frequencies in Tables 1 and 2 sum to 3,558 cities (44 + 43 + 380 + 3,091 = 3,558; 145 + 1,534 + 1,879 = 3,558), whereas the regression and descriptive analytic sample reported in the Abstract and notes to Tables 1, 3, and 4 is N = 3,547 cities across 21 states. 5. OUTCOME BOUNDARY: The outcome captures in-dwelling municipal tap water only (excluding public standpipes outside premises) and does not measure water supply hours/continuity or potability.
raw_response.study_design: City-level longitudinal census first-difference / panel-change study (2001 to 2011) analyzed using two-level nested multilevel linear regression models with state-level random effects (maximum likelihood estimation, state-clustered standard errors) and descriptive comparisons of group means.
raw_response.unit_and_sample_size: Statutory urban local governments (cities and towns) in India enumerated in both the 2001 and 2011 Censuses; primary analytic sample N = 3,547 cities and towns nested within 21 Indian states (excludes Union Territories and 7 northeastern states due to missing data; note that category frequency counts in Tables 1 and 2 sum to 3,558 cities).
